l: information retrieval, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, C. Discussion on GraphRAG
s: Knowledge retrieval in GraphRAG uses the connections and hierarchical organization of graph knowledge bases rather than examining isolated information pieces. Community summaries provide local perspectives that are synthesized into broader answers, improving the breadth and diversity of insights for global questions.

l: knowledge integration, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, C. Discussion on GraphRAG
s: Knowledge integration allows users to inject domain-specific knowledge into large language models. Its design must account for computational overhead, graph-structured input, and the challenges of handling large-scale graphs.

l: large language model, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, C. Discussion on GraphRAG
s: Large language models are used by city planners in the GraphRAG planning analogy to divide source documents, identify element instances, create summaries, and produce community reports. They are not inherently equipped to process graph-structured data, and their input-length limits make large graph problems difficult to handle.

l: knowledge base, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, C. Discussion on GraphRAG
s: A GraphRAG knowledge base integrates multiple data sources and can incorporate ontologies and semantic schemas. Its planning phase creates a hierarchical representation from individual elements and communities to community reports, which are later used for retrieval.

l: computational overhead, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, C. Discussion on GraphRAG
s: Computational overhead increases when retrieved text consumes input length and when graph elements such as nodes, triples, and paths must be processed and managed. Because prompt processing time scales quadratically with prompt length, large retrieved texts can substantially increase the cost and processing time of large language models.

l: fine-tuning, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, C. Discussion on GraphRAG
s: Fine-tuning is presented as a way to permanently integrate domain-specific knowledge into large language models. It can reduce reliance on extensive external text retrieval, potentially improving response speed and reducing time and financial costs, although large language model fine-tuning may require hundreds of gigabytes of memory.

l: graph-structured input, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, C. Discussion on GraphRAG
s: Graph-structured input is difficult for large language models because they commonly convert graph data into natural-language descriptions, which do not fully convey complex geometric properties. Accurate modeling of graph-structured input is important for tasks such as node classification, link prediction, and increasingly complex graph reasoning.

l: large-scale graph, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, C. Discussion on GraphRAG
s: Large-scale graphs create scalability challenges because their numbers of nodes and edges may exceed the input-length limits of large language models. Efficiently managing large-scale graph problems is identified as an important research area for applications including social network analysis, bioinformatics, and knowledge graph construction.

l: A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, D. Traditional RAG Pipeline
s: The unit explains how RAG uses information retrieved from pre-constructed external knowledge bases to guide large language models toward more credible and accurate content. It describes the traditional RAG pipeline as comprising knowledge organization, knowledge retrieval, and knowledge integration. The unit covers chunking, embeddings, vector databases, retrieval methods such as k-nearest neighbor retrieval and BM25, and techniques for filtering, integrating, compressing, and efficiently using retrieved knowledge. It also presents hierarchical indexing as an early structured approach that helped inspire GraphRAG.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, D. Traditional RAG Pipeline
s: RAG retrieves relevant information from external knowledge bases and uses it to prompt large language models. It can make generated content more substantiated and accurate while minimizing hallucinations and inconsistencies.

l: traditional RAG pipeline, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, D. Traditional RAG Pipeline
s: The traditional RAG pipeline consists of knowledge organization, knowledge retrieval, and knowledge integration. These stages prepare external knowledge, select relevant information, and use it to support generated responses.

l: knowledge organization, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, D. Traditional RAG Pipeline
s: Knowledge organization structures and prepares external repositories for rapid and relevant retrieval. It includes granularity optimization through chunking and indexing optimization through metadata addition and hierarchical indexing.

l: knowledge retrieval, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, D. Traditional RAG Pipeline
s: Knowledge retrieval accesses pre-organized repositories to select information that improves generated outputs. It includes methods such as k-nearest neighbor retrieval, TF-IDF, BM25, query expansion, re-ranking, self-supervised retriever training, active retrieval, and external API use.

l: knowledge integration, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, D. Traditional RAG Pipeline
s: Knowledge integration synthesizes retrieved and inherent knowledge into coherent and accurate responses. It uses filtering, self-reflection, selective retrieval, compression, pre-encoding, caching, and parallel retrieval and generation to improve quality and efficiency.

l: large language model, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, D. Traditional RAG Pipeline
s: A large language model is prompted with retrieved information to construct more credible reasoning chains and generate informed content. It can also assess retrieved and generated content, decide when retrieval is necessary, and generate labels or memory used by RAG methods.

l: external knowledge bases, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, D. Traditional RAG Pipeline
s: An external knowledge base provides information that RAG retrieves in response to a query. External sources such as Wikipedia and Google Search APIs can broaden retrieval and provide more current information.

l: text corpus, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, D. Traditional RAG Pipeline
s: A text corpus is split into manageable units during knowledge organization. Its contents can also be pre-encoded or indexed to support efficient retrieval.

l: text chunk, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, D. Traditional RAG Pipeline
s: A text chunk is a manageable segment of a larger text corpus. It is transformed into an embedding, and metadata such as titles, timestamps, categories, and keywords may be attached to it for filtering and re-ranking.

l: embedding model, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, D. Traditional RAG Pipeline
s: An embedding model transforms text chunks into embeddings. Sentence transformers can also provide representations for approximate neighbor identification before BM25 re-ranking.

l: embedding, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, D. Traditional RAG Pipeline
s: An embedding represents an original text chunk and serves as a key in a vector database. Embeddings enable distance-based semantic search for relevant content.

l: vector database, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, D. Traditional RAG Pipeline
s: A vector database stores embeddings associated with original text chunks. It supports efficient lookup and retrieval through distance-based search in semantic space.

l: chunking strategy, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, D. Traditional RAG Pipeline
s: A chunking strategy divides documents according to token limits while attempting to preserve semantic completeness and optimize context length. Recursive splits, sliding windows, and Small-to-Big are identified as chunking strategies.

l: GraphRAG, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, D. Traditional RAG Pipeline
s: GraphRAG is presented as a successor to tree-like hierarchical indexing methods for structured knowledge organization. Its development was inspired by earlier efforts to organize knowledge through parent-child relationships and summaries.

l: K-nearest neighbor retrieval, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, D. Traditional RAG Pipeline
s: K-nearest neighbor retrieval is used to retrieve relevant content from organized knowledge repositories. RETRO applies it by calculating L2 distance to extract approximate relevant neighbors from a key-value database.

l: Best Matching 25, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, D. Traditional RAG Pipeline
s: Best matching 25, also called BM25, is a retrieval method used to identify relevant content. It can be combined with query expansion, re-ranking, or sentence-transformer representations to improve accuracy and computational efficiency.

l: retrieval techniques, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, D. Traditional RAG Pipeline
s: Retrieval selects external information that can improve the quality of generated outputs. The unit describes retrieval as being enhanced through query expansion, re-ranking, dynamic timing, filtering, external APIs, and methods that determine whether retrieval is needed.

l: generation, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, D. Traditional RAG Pipeline
s: Generation uses retrieved and inherent knowledge to produce responses through a large language model. The unit describes efforts to make generation more accurate and efficient through context filtering, self-reflection, compression, caching, and concurrent retrieval.

l: hallucination, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, D. Traditional RAG Pipeline
s: RAG is described as reducing hallucinations by grounding generation in retrieved information. Filtering irrelevant content, assessing retrieved material, and excluding distracting elements are presented as ways to mitigate hallucination risks.

l: RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Abstract
s: The unit examines how Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) affects the safety of large language models (LLMs) compared with non-RAG frameworks. A comparative analysis of eleven LLMs finds that RAG can make models less safe and alter their safety profile. The analysis shows that unsafe generations can occur even when both the models and retrieved documents are safe. It also finds that existing red-teaming methods are less effective for RAG settings than for non-RAG settings, highlighting the need for RAG-specific safety research.

l: AI safety, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Abstract
s: AI safety work has focused primarily on standard LLMs, leaving the effects of RAG use cases less understood. The unit argues that safety research should be tailored specifically to RAG LLMs.

l: red teaming, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Abstract
s: Red teaming is used as part of efforts to ensure LLM safety. Existing red-teaming methods are less effective in RAG settings than in non-RAG settings.

l: RAG, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Abstract
s: RAG can make models less safe and change their safety profile. The unit finds that even combinations of safe models and safe documents can produce unsafe generations.

l: LLMs, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Abstract
s: The study conducts a comparative analysis of RAG and non-RAG frameworks using eleven LLMs. It finds that their safety can change when they are used with RAG.

l: non-RAG setting, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Abstract
s: Non-RAG frameworks are compared with RAG frameworks across eleven LLMs. Red-teaming methods perform better in non-RAG settings than in RAG settings.

l: safety profiles, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Abstract
s: RAG can change a model's safety profile and make the model less safe. The unit investigates causes of this change.

l: unsafe responses, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Abstract
s: Unsafe generations can result from combinations of safe models with safe documents in a RAG setting.

l: red-teaming methods for RAG, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Abstract
s: Existing red-teaming methods are evaluated in RAG settings and found to be less effective than when used for non-RAG settings. The unit highlights the need for methods specifically designed for RAG LLMs.

l: RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Introduction
s: The introduction examines whether Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are safer than non-RAG large language models when answering harmful questions. The authors compare eleven popular models on more than 5,000 harmful questions and find that RAG can introduce unsafe behavior even when the model and retrieved documents are safe. For example, Llama-3-8B's unsafe responses increase from 0.3% to 9.2% in the RAG setting. The authors also find that existing red-teaming methods may fail against RAG-based models and argue that RAG-specific methods are needed.

l: LLMs, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Introduction
s: Large language models can support many tasks but are susceptible to creating unsafe content. The unit examines their safety in non-RAG and RAG settings.

l: unsafe content, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Introduction
s: Unsafe content includes harmful, illegal, offensive, and unethical material, including misinformation and threats to personal safety and privacy. Large language models may generate such content.

l: safety concerns, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Introduction
s: Safety concerns about large language models can expose service providers to legal risks and undermine public trust in AI. The unit discusses safety fine-tuning, guardrails, and red teaming as responses to these concerns.

l: red teaming, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Introduction
s: Red teaming probes large language models with prompts to expose vulnerabilities, including jailbreaking attempts. The unit finds that methods designed for non-RAG settings may be ineffective for RAG-based models.

l: jailbreaking, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Introduction
s: Jailbreaking is described as a type of vulnerability that red teaming attempts to expose. Adversarial prompts that jailbreak an LLM in a non-RAG setting may fail in a RAG setting.

l: RAG, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Introduction
s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation identifies relevant documents from a corpus and provides them to a large language model to support a response. The unit finds that RAG can make relatively safe models unsafe, even when the retrieved documents are safe.

l: retrieved documents, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Introduction
s: Retrieved documents influence the responses of RAG-based models and can provide grounding, updated information, and attribution. The unit finds that safe retrieved documents do not guarantee safe generations.

l: corpus, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Introduction
s: A corpus supplies documents for retrieval in a RAG system. The unit considers whether securing the corpus guarantees system safety and concludes that using a safe corpus alone does not guarantee safety.

l: infusion attacks, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Introduction
s: Infusion attacks are identified as a main focus of recent work on RAG safety. In these attacks, vulnerabilities come from harmful documents injected into the source corpus.

l: corpus poisoning, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Introduction
s: Corpus poisoning is described as a means of injecting harmful documents into a source corpus, enabling infusion attacks. The unit distinguishes this issue from unsafe behavior that can arise even with a safe corpus.

l: harmful questions, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Introduction
s: The study evaluates eleven popular large language models on more than 5,000 harmful questions. It assumes that these questions should not be answered in either RAG or non-RAG settings.

l: unsafe responses, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Introduction
s: Unsafe responses increase when some models are used with RAG. For Llama-3-8B, the rate rises from 0.3% in the non-RAG setting to 9.2% in the RAG setting.

l: Llama-3-8B, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Introduction
s: Llama-3-8B is presented as a relatively safe model that becomes unsafe in the RAG setting. Its unsafe responses increase from 0.3% to 9.2%, and it can produce unsafe generations even when combined with safe documents.

l: adversarial prompts, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Introduction
s: Adversarial prompts that can jailbreak a model without RAG fail in the RAG setting. Optimizing them based on retrieved documents improves their effectiveness, but differences between documents used in training and testing remain a problem.

l: RAG capability, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Introduction
s: RAG capability is one of three factors examined as influencing model safety, alongside model safety and the safety of retrieved documents. The unit finds that all three factors affect safety.

l: safety profiles, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Introduction
s: The study assesses the safety profiles of eleven popular large language models on more than 5,000 harmful questions. It finds that RAG introduces unsafe behaviors across nearly every safety category.

l: RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Related Work
s: The unit reviews safety research on LLMs, including fine-tuning, system-level guardrails, red-teaming, controllable generation, interpretability, unlearning, and benchmark evaluation. It notes that most safety studies focus on non-RAG settings, while safety research on RAG LLMs emphasizes corpus poisoning and also examines corpus leakage, retriever robustness, and document perturbations. The unit focuses on RAG scenarios with a carefully controlled corpus and relates them to the safety of LLM agents using tools. It also surveys red-teaming and states that no red-teaming methods have been designed specifically for RAG LLMs.

l: LLMs, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Related Work
s: LLMs are aligned with human values through supervised learning, RLHF, safety-specific examples, system-level guardrails, controllable safe generation, interpretability, unlearning, and safety evaluation. Red-teaming is used to identify their vulnerabilities.

l: red teaming, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Related Work
s: Red-teaming identifies vulnerabilities in LLMs, commonly by jailbreaking them with human-designed tests or LLM-generated prompts. The unit notes that no red-teaming methods have been designed specifically for RAG LLMs.

l: non-RAG setting, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Related Work
s: Most studies on LLM safety focus on non-RAG settings.

l: RAG LLMs, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Related Work
s: Research on RAG LLM safety mainly focuses on corpus poisoning, while also addressing corpus leakage, retriever robustness to noise, and resilience to document perturbations. The unit considers RAG LLMs in scenarios where the corpus is carefully controlled.

l: corpus poisoning, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Related Work
s: Corpus poisoning is a threat to RAG LLMs in which injecting harmful documents leads to unsafe outputs.

l: corpus, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Related Work
s: The unit focuses on a common RAG scenario in which the corpus is carefully controlled.

l: retriever, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Related Work
s: A retriever's robustness to noise is identified as a safety concern in RAG systems. A retriever is also described as a special tool used by LLM agents.

l: jailbreaking methods, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Related Work
s: Jailbreaking LLMs is a common part of red-teaming and is used to expose vulnerabilities through human-designed tests or LLM-generated prompts.

s: The unit defines a standard RAG pipeline as consisting of an LLM G and a retriever R, such as BM25 or a dense retriever. s: The standard RAG pipeline contains an LLM G and a retriever R. It retrieves relevant documents for a user query and supplies them to the LLM to generate a response.

s: RAG uses retrieved documents as context for LLM generation. Most LLMs in the RAG setting exhibit a significantly higher percentage of unsafe responses than in the non-RAG setting.

s: The LLM G takes an instruction, retrieved documents, and a user query as input to generate a response. In a standard non-RAG pipeline, it instead relies on knowledge stored in the model.

l: retriever, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Definitions
s: The retriever R first retrieves the top k most relevant documents from a corpus for a given user query. It may be sparse, such as BM25, or dense.

l: user query, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Definitions
s: The user query is provided to the retriever to identify relevant documents and is then supplied to the LLM along with the retrieved documents.

s: The retrieved documents are the top k documents selected by the retriever from the corpus. They provide context for the LLM's generation.

s: The response is generated by the LLM from the instruction, retrieved documents, and user query in a RAG pipeline. In the non-RAG pipeline, it is generated from a different instruction and the query.

l: template, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models, Definitions

s: The standard non-RAG LLM pipeline depends on knowledge stored in the model rather than retrieved documents. It generates a response from a different instruction and the user query.

s: The unit reports a large-scale evaluation of eleven LLMs comparing non-RAG, RAG (Docs), and RAG (Docs + Model Knowledge) settings on 5,592 harmful questions. It finds that RAG-based LLMs are generally not safer: eight of eleven models show markedly different safety behavior, often with increased unsafe responses, including Llama-3-8B-Instruct, large models, and GPT-4o. RAG also changes models’ risk profiles in a model-dependent way, with Llama-3-8B-Instruct becoming vulnerable across all 16 risk categories. The evaluation uses BM25 over English Wikipedia and Llama Guard 2 to judge response safety.

l: GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Abstract
s: The abstract introduces Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GRAG) as an approach for handling networked documents that Naive Retrieval-Augmented Generation overlooks. GRAG retrieves textual subgraphs using a divide-and-conquer strategy that finds the optimal subgraph structure in linear time. It integrates textual graphs into Large Language Models through complementary text and graph views for graph context-aware generation. l: GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Introduction
s: The introduction concerns how Large Language Models can use networked documents through Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GRAG). It explains that traditional Retrieval-Augmented Generation retrieves individual documents by text similarity, whereas GRAG retrieves relevant textual subgraphs and incorporates both textual and topological information into generation. GRAG addresses retrieval through ego-graph retrieval followed by graph soft pruning, and addresses generation through hierarchical text descriptions, hard prompts, and soft prompts. Experiments on graph multi-hop reasoning tasks show that GRAG outperforms RAG-based retrievers and LLM baselines, with frozen LLMs using GRAG outperforming fine-tuned LLMs on all tasks.
